questions.question: Describe the structure of one sixty-mark theory question in the Geography papers, including where the paragraph question fits and how it is marked.
questions.expected_answer: Each sixty-mark question opens with fifteen marks of short objective items such as multiple choice, matching and one-word answers, followed by three subquestions of fifteen marks each built on source material and stepped from two-mark definitions to longer explanations. Hidden within the question is an eight-mark paragraph, marked as four ideas at two marks each, which must be written in full sentences and is pitched at middle and higher cognitive order.

questions.question: Using the synoptic chart walkthrough, explain how mark allocations should control the length of your answers, with examples.
questions.expected_answer: The mark allocation is the instruction for answer length: a one-times-two identification like naming the mid-latitude cyclone needs one precise line; a two-times-two question like giving winter evidence needs two developed facts; a three-times-two description like the cold front sequence needs three developed sentences covering before, during and after the front. Writing a paragraph for a two-mark question wastes exam effort, and writing one line for a six-mark question leaves marks unclaimed.

questions.question: Write out the four-move recipe for the eight-mark paragraph question and apply it to the informal settlements task from the lesson.
questions.expected_answer: Move one: obey the instruction verb, here 'suggest', which demands solutions. Move two: plan four ideas as keywords, such as in-situ upgrading, secure tenure, releasing well-located land, and community partnership. Move three: write one full sentence per idea, developing each with a because-clause — for example, upgrading in situ provides water, sanitation and electricity while keeping communities intact. Move four: use the topic's own vocabulary, like tenure and in-situ upgrading, so each of the four developed ideas earns its two marks.
